answer: Pedestrian deaths in NYC fell from a 13-year high of 176 in 2013 to 119 in 2025, averaging 130 per year. The decline was uneven: 2016 saw a rebound to 149, 2020 was the lowest year at 101 (101 deaths, ~29% below the 2013 peak), and the count has hovered in the 107–135 range since 2021.

answer: Across 2013–2025 NYC logged 2,132,218 crashes, and they are not spread evenly over the week: Friday is the peak with 338,800 crashes (15.9%, ~500 per day) and Sunday the trough with 257,544 (12.1%, ~380 per day) — a 31% Friday-over-Sunday gap; Thursday (318,376) and Tuesday (313,488) follow, while Saturday (288,381) falls below the weekday average. The pattern is stable: Friday ranked highest and Sunday lowest in every one of the 13 years, and it holds whether you use raw totals or per-day averages (weekday counts differ by only 678 vs 679 occurrences).

answer: Motorist deaths outnumber cyclist deaths every year, roughly 5 to 1 on average (106 vs 21 per year, 2013-2025). Motorist deaths fell from 110 (2013) to a low of 72 (2016), then spiked to 139 in 2020 and stayed elevated (111-134) through 2024 before dropping to 81 in 2025. Cyclist deaths trended the other way overall — 11 in 2013 to 23 in 2025, with peaks of 31 in 2019 and 2023 and a low of 10 in 2018 — so the gap has narrowed in recent years, though motorist deaths still exceed cyclist deaths by about 4-5x.

answer: Yes — NYC streets are far deadlier after dark, though less busy. Among 2.27M police-reported crashes (2012–mid-2026), crashes between 10pm and 6am kill 3.5 people per 1,000 crashes vs 1.2 in daytime — about 2.9× as deadly (0.33% vs 0.12% of crashes are fatal; 0.40 vs 0.32 injuries per crash). Night sees only 17% of crashes but 37% of deaths, with lethality peaking at 4am (6.4 deaths per 1,000 crashes, ~7× the midday rate). Most crashes and deaths still occur in daytime simply because there is far more traffic; per crash, a nighttime trip is roughly three times as likely to end in a death, a gap that holds in every recent year. (Severity per crash is used because traffic-exposure data is unavailable; slight under-reporting of minor nighttime crashes could inflate the ratio somewhat, but death counts are hard numbers.)
